# Automatic differentiation

`f∂X` gives the derivative of `f` at `X`. `∂` works by running `f`. It differentiates through the primitives that `f` calls, inside dfns, trains and operators alike. A function needs no special form to be differentiated. `⊼` squares its argument. `+/⊼` sums the squares:

```bpl
⊼∂3                          ⍝ 6
(+/⊼)∂ 1 2 3                 ⍝ 2 4 6
```

The [`∂` page](glyphs/partial.qmd) lists what `∂` differentiates and the errors it gives.

## What `∂` gives

The Jacobian of `f` at `X` holds the derivative of each item of `f X` with respect to each number in `X`. `f∂X` gives it, with the keys, axis names and nesting of the outer product `(f X)×⊗X`. A function that gives a number has a Jacobian with `X`'s structure: its gradient. A record argument gives a record gradient, with the record's keys. `cart` converts polar coordinates to Cartesian ones. Its Jacobian has a row for each result and a column for each argument:

```bpl
cart←{[r t]←⍵ ⋄ [r×2○t r×1○t]} ⋄ cart∂ 2 0.5   ⍝ [0.8775825619 ¯0.9588510772⋄0.4794255386 1.755165124]
p←["w":2 "b":1] ⋄ {3×⍵.w + ⍵.b}∂ p               ⍝ ["w":3 "b":1]
```

`W f∂ X` differentiates `W f X` with respect to `X`. The left argument holds what isn't differentiated, such as training data:

```bpl
3 {⍺×⍵×⍵}∂ 2                ⍝ 12
```

A JVP is the derivative of `f` at `x` in a direction `t`. `{f x+⍵×t}∂0` computes it by differentiating along one number. A vector–Jacobian product multiplies a vector `u` by the Jacobian. `{+/u×f⍵}∂ x` computes it by differentiating a sum. Neither builds the Jacobian. With `t` and `u` both `1 0`, the JVP gives the Jacobian's first column. The vector–Jacobian product gives its first row:

```bpl
f←{[x y]←⍵ ⋄ [x×y x+y]} ⋄ x←2 3
f∂ x                        ⍝ [3 2⋄1 1]
t←1 0 ⋄ {f x+⍵×t}∂0         ⍝ 3 1
u←1 0 ⋄ {+/u×f⍵}∂ x         ⍝ 3 2
```

For a function that works item by item, such as the sine `1○`, `f∂⍤0` gives the derivative at each item. Differentiating along one number gives the same values in one pass:

```bpl
x←0 0.5 1
1○∂⍤0 x                     ⍝ 1 0.8775825619 0.5403023059
{1○x+⍵}∂0                   ⍝ 1 0.8775825619 0.5403023059
```

`f∂∂` is `∂` applied to `f∂`. It gives second and mixed derivatives, such as the matrix of mixed derivatives of `×/`, the product of the items. Differentiated numbers promote to real floating-point values:

```bpl
{⍵×⍵×⍵}∂∂∂2                  ⍝ 6
×/∂∂ 2 3                     ⍝ [0 1⋄1 0]
⊼∂3ₓ                         ⍝ 6
```

## Forward mode

Where `X` holds one number, `∂` runs `f` once, in forward mode. Every value that depends on `X` carries its derivative with respect to `X` beside it, as a dual number. `∂` starts the pass by making `X` a dual whose derivative is 1. A call on duals gives a dual. A pervasive function, such as `×` or `*`, finds its result's derivative by the chain rule, from a table of its partial derivatives. `⍺×⍵` has the partials `⍵` and `⍺`. `*⍵` has the partial `*⍵`, its own result. `∂` returns the derivative that the final result carries.

Each `∂` call tags the duals it makes. A call reads only the derivatives with its own tag. Under nested `∂`, as in `{⍵×⍵×⍵}∂∂∂2`, a value is a dual of a dual of a dual. Julia's ForwardDiff tags its dual numbers in the same way.

Functions that move items, such as reshape, transpose, take and windows, move each item's derivative with the item. Comparisons, floor, `⍳`, grade and other functions whose results are counts, positions or Booleans give results with no derivative.

## Reverse mode

Forward mode takes one pass for each number in `X`. A network with a million parameters would take a million passes. Where `X` holds more than one number, `∂` instead runs `f` once with a record in place of each derivative. A record's items are never computed. Each call on a record adds a linear step to it, built from the same partial derivatives that forward mode uses. The steps are few: scaling by a coefficient, adding, copying from positions, broadcasting, folding by `+`, and matrix products with a constant. When `f` returns, the record holds the linearisation of `f` at `X`. That's the linear map from a small change in `X` to the change it causes in `f X`.

`∂` then reads the Jacobian from the record. A run through the record backwards, through each step's transpose in reverse order, gives one row of the Jacobian. A run forwards gives one column. `∂` takes the direction that needs fewer runs. It makes them as one batched run, whose inputs are the rows or columns of an identity matrix, as JAX's `jacrev` maps `vjp` over a basis. A function that gives a number, such as a loss, needs one backward run. Its gradient costs a small multiple of one run of `f`, however many numbers `X` holds. Dex and JAX also build reverse mode as the transpose of a linearisation. One set of tangent rules then serves both modes.

Each linear step has one transpose:

| Step | Transpose |
|---|---|
| Scaling by a coefficient | Scaling by the same coefficient |
| Adding two values | The same gradient to each value |
| A broadcast | A sum over the broadcast axes |
| A fold by `+` along an axis | A broadcast along that axis |
| A copy that reads each item at most once, such as a transpose, reverse, take or drop | A copy back through the inverse map |
| A sum over windows that move by 1 | A sliding sum |
| Windows that move by more than 1 | Each window's gradient, added back where the window read |
| A selection that can repeat positions | An accumulation into those positions |
| A matrix product with a constant | A matrix product with the constant's transpose |

The transposes work on whole arrays, as the steps do. The transpose of a selection adds each gradient into the position that it was read from. It never builds an array of zeros with a one at each position read. In this example, `3↕` gives windows of 3. The first function reads item 0 twice and never reads item 1. In the second, the middle items appear in more of the windows:

```bpl
0 0 2 {+/⊼⍵.[⍺]}∂ 1 2 3     ⍝ 4 0 6
{+/,⊼3↕⍵}∂ 1 2 3 4 5        ⍝ 2 8 18 16 10
```

Folds and matrix functions have rules of their own. `×/` divides the product by each item to find that item's derivative, with zeros counted apart. `⌈/` and `⌊/` take the derivative of the item that they pick. `⌹` and the determinant `-.×` take their derivatives from one factorization of the matrix.

The record keeps the values that its steps need, such as the coefficients of its scalings, until `∂` returns. Its memory grows with the work that `f` does.

## Rules of your own

`f∂←g` attaches `g` as the derivative of `f`. `g` is a JVP rule: `T g X` gives the derivative of `f` at `X` in the direction `T`. Forward mode calls `g` with the tangent as `T`. Reverse mode records the steps that `g` takes on `T`, then transposes them, as JAX transposes a `custom_jvp` rule. One rule serves both modes. A straight-through estimator, which treats rounding as if its derivative were 1, is such a rule:

```bpl
r←{⍵×⍵} ⋄ r∂←{⍺×2×⍵}
{1+r⍵}∂3                    ⍝ 6
ste←{⌊⍵} ⋄ ste∂←{⍺}
{+/ste⍵×2}∂ 1.5 2.5         ⍝ 2 2
```

`•detach X` gives `X` with every derivative removed. `∂` then treats it as a constant, as JAX treats the result of `stop_gradient`. `⊢×•detach` multiplies its argument by a detached copy of itself. Its derivative at 3 is the copy's value, 3, where `⊼∂3` gives 6:

```bpl
(⊢×•detach)∂3                ⍝ 3
```

A value that `f` writes to a name outside itself loses its derivatives when `∂` returns. A function gives the same values with and without `∂`.

## Writes

`∂` differentiates indexed, sliced and masked replacement and additive updates on native floating arrays. The update must keep the array's shape. The replacement can depend on the differentiated input:

```bpl
{v←⍵ ⋄ v.[0]←0 ⋄ +/v}∂1 2 3               ⍝ 0 1 1
{v←⍵ ⋄ v.[0]+←⍵.[1] ⋄ +/v}∂1 2 3         ⍝ 1 2 1
{v←⍵ ⋄ v.[[0 2]]←+/⍵ ⋄ +/v}∂1 2 3        ⍝ 2 3 2
```

Positions and masks are fixed choices during differentiation. `∂` does not differentiate which positions were chosen. Replacement requires distinct destinations. Additive updates accumulate every occurrence of a repeated destination. A broadcast replacement's gradient sums back to the replacement's original shape, as the third example shows.

These rules also apply to selecting [Under](glyphs/at.qmd). An update on differentiated data that changes the array's shape or nesting, or uses a host-valued replacement, gives UNSUPPORTED ERROR. Ordinary [nested-item replacement](glyphs/left-arrow.qmd#write-support) can change an item's shape without differentiating the write.

## Programs: trace once, replay

A training loop repeatedly differentiates the same loss. Here a network with 16 tanh units (`7○`) fits 64 points of sin 3x (`1○3×x`) in 200 steps of gradient descent on a record of parameters:

```bpl
x←⍳64 ÷ 63 ⋄ y←1○3×x
loss←{[x y]←⍺ ⋄ [w b v c]←⍵ ⋄ h←7○b(+⍤1)x×⊗w ⋄ +/÷≢ ⊼y-c+h+.×v}
p←["w":1○⍳16 "b":16⍴0 "v":0.1×2○⍳16 "c":0]
[x y] loss p                ⍝ 0.5232276475
p←{⍵ - 0.1× [x y]loss∂⍵}⍣200p
[x y] loss p                ⍝ 0.07655752909
```

A recording remembers the graph built by a function call. Later matching calls bind its inputs and build that graph without running the body again. The current arguments, captured free values and bound arrays supply those inputs. They are captured once at the call, not reread from names during deferred execution. Derivative steps use the ordinary graph, including when they are built inside a recorded function.

The cache keys input kinds, ranks, axis names and keys, equalities between lengths, and structural parameters such as operator ranks and permutations. Ordinary data-axis lengths have three classes: 0, 1 and more than 1. A new length in the same class can reuse the recording. The graph's descriptions and read maps are refilled with the actual lengths. A count that decides how many calls Power or a dfn fold unrolls is keyed by its exact value.

Only a read schedules and executes the graph. The scheduler groups elementwise operations and folds into block stages. Intermediates stay within a block where the stage permits it. Native stages compile to machine code with Cranelift when the expected work repays compilation. The browser runs the same stages without the native JIT. `•explain` reports `record` when a call creates a recording and `replay` when it reuses one:

```bpl
sq←{+/⊼⍵} ⋄ sq 1 2 3
(•explain "sq 4 5 6").programs.event      ⍝ ["replay"]
(•explain "sq 4 5 6 7").programs.event    ⍝ ["replay"]
```

Both later calls reuse the recording. Three and four items have the same length class.

A dfn's definition identifies its recordings. Other functions key by structure. Bound arrays and free data are inputs rather than part of that structure. Replacing `w` with new data of the same kind and compatible layout does not require another recording:

```bpl
w←1 2 3 ⋄ (+/w×⊢)4 5 6
w←7 8 9 ⋄ (•explain "(+/w×⊢)4 5 6").programs.event   ⍝ ["replay"]
```

### What stops a trace

Stopping a recording leaves the ordinary call running through the same graph and derivative rules. It does not select a different numerical evaluator. The cache keeps the stop for its signature and structural parameters. `•explain` lists the reason in `stopped`:

- `observing argument data`: a host decision reads an argument's items, as a dfn guard does. A dynamic result kind that cannot be proved from descriptions also requires such a read.
- `host-kind data`: the call needs structure that the recording cannot describe, such as a write that replaces a native number by an array.
- `itemwise batch fallback`: a map must call the body separately for each cell instead of batching it.
- `outer binding write`, `binding or setting effect`, `execute`, `error guard` or `recursion`: the body changes bindings or settings, runs text, catches errors or recurses through a boundary that recording does not hold.
- `runtime renderer metadata` or `drawn name as text`: rendering or text depends on runtime bindings or fresh axis names.
- `retrace limit`: too many variants of a recording's structural read parameters.

Output effects such as `⎕←`, `•time`, `•delay` and `•nput`, and numeric draws with described results, remain in recordings. Replay runs each effect and draw once in order.

A guard on a differentiated value reads its primal value to choose the executed body. It still computes the derivative of that body:

```bpl
pos←{+/⍵ > 0 ? +/⊼⍵ ; 0}
(•explain "pos∂ 1 2 3").stopped.reason
```

Reading a kind or a shape needs no items. Ordinary array counts, such as the number of results from a selection, can be recorded and recomputed at their current lengths. Captured data used to decide graph structure becomes a checked parameter. Runtime positions remain data: replay selects at the current positions. [Assignment](glyphs/left-arrow.qmd#write-support) describes how checked and static writes handle invalid positions.

Under dynamic kinds, an operation such as `√` can return real or complex values. Range proofs use kinds, keyed literals, graph operations and current shapes and counts, never the observed extrema of an input. If those facts do not decide the result kind, the operation reads the relevant data. Recording stops when that read depends on an argument:

```bpl
roots←{+/√⍵}
(•explain "roots 1 2 3").stopped.reason    ⍝ ["observing argument data"]
```

Static kinds fix numeric result kinds from the argument kinds. `√ₐ`, `⍟ₐ` and `*ₐ` select real results under either setting. These forms avoid the data read needed to choose between real and complex results ([Numbers](numbers.qmd#approximate)).

Write fast differentiated code under static kinds, using Agenda (`⍚`) or mask Under (`f@[p]`) for array branches rather than dfn guards. A masked case runs on whole arrays. AD gates its inputs and tangent directions so an inactive infinite slope does not make the gradient NaN. Cases that cannot run masked compact their selected cells and call the original bound function on that group. Both forms use the same graph and derivative rules.

## Index notation

Index notation writes the formula for one element with named indices. BPL runs the formula once, on whole arrays. [Indexing](indexing.ipynb#named-and-fresh-indices) and [`•index`](system/index.qmd) describe it. `∂` differentiates index notation as it differentiates any other code. This matrix product, written with indices, has the same gradient as `+.×`:

```bpl
xu←[2 3]⍴⍳6 ⋄ wu←[3 4]⍴⍳12 ⋄ [b o k]←•index 2 4 3
{+/,⊼⍵.[b k]+.×⍠k⁝wu.[k o]}∂ xu    ⍝ [324 1108 1892⋄1008 3376 5744]
{+/,⊼⍵+.×wu}∂ xu                     ⍝ [324 1108 1892⋄1008 3376 5744]
```

In a program, the indices keep their structure:

- A `+` fold over named axes of a product, where both operands step along every folded axis, runs as a matrix product `+.×`. The folds in its gradient run as products where they meet the same condition.
- A read through positions computed from indices, such as `x.[i+1]`, is a copy through a map. Its transpose reads back through the inverse map.
- A read through positions from data, such as an embedding lookup `E.[ids]`, is a gather. Its transpose adds into the positions that it read.

Each replay of a dfn that uses `•index` gives its result's indices fresh names, as an untraced call does.

BPL's design studied Dex, whose index sets informed `•index`. Two points from Dex's paper hold in BPL's programs. Only nonlinear steps keep values for the transpose. Indexing is linear and keeps none. The transpose of indexing is an accumulation.

## Where the design comes from

JAX, Dex and tinygrad are the role models. Futhark, Dex and Julia set the standard that the design is judged by:

- A gradient costs a small multiple of one run of the function, whatever the number of variables.
- The derivative of a whole-array operation is a whole-array operation.
- One rule for each primitive serves both modes.
- Nested `∂` never confuses its levels.
- Code that isn't differentiated pays nothing for `∂`.

| System | What BPL shares with it |
|---|---|
| JAX | A function traced into a program of primitives, and replayed on later calls. Reverse mode as the transpose of a linearisation. JVP rules that reverse mode transposes, like `custom_jvp` rules. `•detach` as `stop_gradient`. Rank doing the job of `vmap`. |
| Dex | Linearising, then transposing. Indices that name a formula's axes. Accumulation as the transpose of indexing. |
| tinygrad | Lazy arrays: every numerical call builds a pending node, and a read of its items runs the calls it needs, fused. Derivative code that fuses as other code does. Copies, such as a transpose or a slice, whose transposes are copies, not scatters. A program replayed as `TinyJit` replays its kernels. |
| Futhark | One table of partial derivatives for both modes, which BPL's table was mapped from. The rules for folds by `×`, `⌈` and `⌊`. Accumulation as the transpose of a gather. |
| ForwardDiff | Dual numbers with tags, which keep nested derivatives apart. |
| J | `D.`, which gives a Jacobian, and `d.`, which gives the derivative at each item. `f∂` and `f∂⍤0` do these jobs. |

BPL also differs from all of them. `∂` strips its tags from values that escape it, where JAX raises an error when a leaked tracer is used. One operator picks the mode, where JAX offers `jvp`, `vjp`, `jacfwd` and `jacrev`. A Jacobian takes its keys, axis names and records from the rules of outer products. Futhark differentiates its program before running it and recomputes values in reverse mode. BPL differentiates the calls that `f` makes as it runs. It keeps their linear steps instead of recomputing values.

## Iteration and limits

Power (`⍣`) and dfn folds and scans call their bodies through the ordinary function entry. Under `∂`, each call adds primal and linear steps to the same graph. There is no separate loop node or loop-specific derivative program. Reverse mode keeps the values that the transposes need until `∂` returns. A long iteration keeps those values for every step. BPL has no checkpointing pass to trade recomputation for memory, as Futhark does.

`∂` differentiates through the executed iterations of `⍣∞` and `⇄`. It does not use implicit differentiation of the converged answer. Complex differentiation gives UNSUPPORTED ERROR.

Graphs run on the CPU. A GPU backend is planned.
